Leonardo da Vinci

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) brought the empirical ethos of the Renaissance to neuroanatomy. He injected molten wax into ox brain ventricles to produce accurate three-dimensional casts—the first experimental modeling of brain structure. His anatomical sketches, though unpublished in his lifetime, revealed a commitment to observation over ancient authority that would define the scientific revolution to come.

Andreas Vesalius

Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) dismantled Galenic neuroanatomy through direct dissection in De Humani Corporis Fabrica 1. His detailed illustrations of the brain, cranial nerves, and spinal cord established that brain structure is an empirical question, not a matter of philosophical deduction. By revealing how much Galen had gotten wrong by relying on animal dissection, Vesalius demonstrated that the accuracy of any model depends on the quality of the data it is built from. Michel de Montaigne

Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) deployed radical skepticism against the pretensions of human reason 2, 3. Our senses are unreliable, our judgments are shaped by custom and bodily states, and introspection is not transparent self-knowledge but a further act of interpretation. For a world-modeling framework, Montaigne is a reminder that the model is not merely of the external world—it includes a model of the modeler, and that self-model is no less fallible.

Francis Bacon

Francis Bacon (1561–1626) catalogued the systematic ways in which the human mind distorts its picture of reality 4. His four idols—of the Tribe (species-wide perceptual and cognitive biases), Cave (individual biases from experience), Marketplace (distortions from imprecise language), and Theater (distortions from received theories)—constitute a proto-taxonomy of the ways a generative model can be misspecified. Science, for Bacon, is the disciplined correction of the mind’s default model.

Galileo Galilei

Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) drew a distinction between primary qualities (size, shape, number, motion—objective and mathematical) and secondary qualities (color, taste, warmth—subjective and perceiver-dependent) 5. This distinction implies that the world as we experience it is not the world as it is: much of perceptual content is generated by the perceiver, not simply received from the world. The mechanistic philosophy Galileo championed would provide the conceptual framework within which the brain itself could be understood as a physical mechanism.

Juan Luis Vives

Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540) produced one of the most remarkably modern psychological works of the Renaissance in De Anima et Vita 6. Rather than speculating about what the soul is, Vives proposed to investigate what it does—its operations, and in particular the associative mechanisms of memory. He described how sensory experiences become linked through contiguity, resemblance, and emotional salience, forming networks of association that determine recall and shape the flow of thought. This operational, mechanistic approach to mental processes—investigating function rather than metaphysical essence—anticipates the functionalist turn by four centuries, and his emphasis on learned associative structure presages connectionist models of memory.

Bernardino Telesio

Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588) broke with Aristotelian scholasticism through a radical empiricism in De Rerum Natura iuxta Propria Principia 7. All knowledge, he insisted, originates in sensus (sensation), which is not a passive reception but an active response of the spiritus—a subtle material substance pervading the nervous system—to external stimulation. The soul itself is material, a warm, thin substance housed in the brain’s ventricles, and cognition is the spiritus’s capacity to detect similarities and differences among sensory impacts. In grounding all mental life in the reactive dynamics of a material nervous substance, Telesio sketched a picture of the mind as a physical system whose fundamental operation is the discrimination and classification of sensory patterns—a pattern recognizer built from matter.
